All walkthroughs / Health organisation

Health organisation · Cardiology

Lock what identifies a person, and read it only with permission

A data engineer seals a table of appointments from two files, so that each patient’s name and reason for visit are locked under a key of their own. The engineer is refused the locked values, asks for five rows, and the custodian of the owning department decides. The platform reports which readable columns could single someone out, and a privacy auditor then checks how everything was used without seeing a single name.

How to read this page

  • Every step is one screen, or one moment, in a real run. The label under the title names where it happens, and the step reads in the same order each time: what is happening, the evidence, and then what to look for in it.
  • Screenshots are real pictures of the Munitas console, the web app that people open in a browser. Click any picture to enlarge it.
  • Every name of a person, patient or card holder in the example data is invented, and every screenshot is unedited apart from being cropped to the part that matters.

Words used on this page

Organisation
A company or hospital group that uses Munitas. Each organisation sees only its own data.
Department
A team inside an organisation that owns some of its data, such as Cardiology.
Dataset
A named collection of records, such as a table of patient admissions.
Custodian
A person who holds the data custodian role, which allows deciding who may read data. A custodian decides for the departments they are an approver for.
Department approver
A custodian who is listed for one department and may approve access to its data and confirm claims about it. A department can have several, and any one of them can act on their own.
Sealed
Finished and closed for good, so that it can never be edited.
Privacy contract
A file that says, column by column, how identifying each column of a table is and what is done to it when the table is sealed, and how to find the person each row is about.
Locked column
A column whose values are scrambled under a key made for each person. Reading them back needs permission. Destroying a person’s key later makes their values unreadable for good, while the sealed table itself never changes.
Person code
A label that stands for one person and means nothing on its own. It replaces the number that identified them.
Locked-column lease
Permission, decided by an approver of the owning department, to read a few rows of a table’s locked columns for a few days, for a stated purpose. It opens only those rows, never the whole table.
Small group
A combination of readable columns, such as postcode and age band, shared by only a few people, so that one of them could be singled out even though no column names anybody.
Privacy auditor
A person who checks how locked data was used. The role reads records of use and no personal data.
Data protection officer
A person who watches how an organisation handles personal data. The role decides nothing about who may read it.
Version
One sealed state of a dataset. Changing the contents means making a new version, never editing an old one.
Role
A named set of permissions that a person can hold, such as the permission to decide who may read a department’s data.
Lease
Permission, given by the custodian, to read one dataset for one stated purpose and for a limited time.
De-identification reviewer
A role that allows a person to review data from which identifying details have been removed, and to decide whether it may be released.

PART ONE

Devi seals a table of appointments from two files

A dataset is a registered, owned collection of data. Sealed means finished and closed for good, so that it can never be edited. This part shows a table of people’s records being sealed in a way that locks what identifies each person, while the table itself stays exactly as sealed.

1
Devi
Devi is asked whether anyone will ever need to be erased from this data
Munitas console · Bring data into a dataset · /datasets/<id>/ingest

The dataset on this page is owned by the Cardiology department of the Health organisation. A department is the team inside an organisation that owns some of its data. Nothing in the dataset is readable yet. Devi is a data engineer, a role that may bring data in. Before any file can be added, the page asks one question: will anyone ever need to erase one person from this data? The answer has to be given now, because locking cannot be added after the upload. The first choice, which is selected when the page opens, stores the files exactly as they are, and nothing in them is locked.

A box titled “Will you ever need to erase one person from this data?” has two choices. “No. Store the files as they are.” is selected, and the usual Upload files area is below it.
2
Devi
Devi answers yes, and chooses to bring in a table of people’s records
Munitas console · Bring data into a dataset · /datasets/<id>/ingest

Devi answers yes. The page explains what that means: the data of each person is locked under a key made for that person, and erasing a person destroys their key, so what was locked for them can never be read again. It also says that locked data is hidden and not anonymised, because it is still personal data until the person is erased. Devi then says what is being brought in, a table of people’s records. The upload area is replaced by two files: a privacy contract, which says column by column how identifying each column is and what is done to it when the table is sealed, and the rows as a CSV file, which is a plain text table with one row on each line and the column names on the first line.

“Yes. Lock what identifies a person, with one key for each person.” is selected, and under “What are you bringing in?” the choice A table of people’s records is selected. Two file choosers, The contract and The rows, both read No file chosen. The button Seal as a table is greyed out, and the text names the limits: 20,000 rows and 5 MB.
3
Devi
A rows file with two mistakes is refused, with both listed
Munitas console · Bring data into a dataset · the table option

Devi chooses the contract and a rows file in which one date has been replaced by the words ‘not a date’ and one patient number has been removed. Pressing Seal as a table is the check. Nothing is sealed, and every problem is listed with the row it belongs to, so that one attempt shows all of them instead of one at a time.

A red box reads Nothing was sealed. Fix these first: and lists two problems. The first is A-1001: seen_on is ‘not a date’, which is not a date written like 2026-03-31. The second is A-1002: names nobody, because patient_number (the patient number) is empty. The file names under the choosers end in contract.yaml and mistakes.csv.
4
Devi
With the right rows file, the table is sealed
Munitas console · Bring data into a dataset · the table option

Devi replaces the rows file with the correct one. For each of the 20 people in it, the platform makes a key of their own and uses it to scramble that person’s name and reason for visit. These are the locked columns. The number that identified each patient is replaced by a person code, a label that stands for one person and means nothing on its own. The platform also counts how many different people share each combination of the columns that stay readable, and reports it.

A green box reads Sealed as version 1: 23 rows about 20 people. It says the identifying values are locked, each under a key made for that person. A line below reads 12 people sit in a group smaller than 5. It did not stop the seal. The link Open this version leads to the sealed table.
5
Devi
The version page lists every column and what was done to it
Munitas console · Version detail · /versions/<id>

The Locked columns section lists each column, how identifying it is, and what was done to it. It never shows a value. patient_name and reason_for_visit are locked. patient_number was replaced by a person code. postcode and age_band stay readable, because researchers need them, but together they could identify someone, which is what the small groups report is about.

patient_name and reason_for_visit carry the label Locked under the person’s key, and patient_number reads Replaced by a person code. The footnote reads 23 rows. Under Your access there is a form, and no name, number or reason for a visit appears anywhere on the page.
PART TWO

Devi cannot read what is locked, so Devi asks

A department approver is a data custodian who is listed for one department and may decide who reads its data. A locked-column lease is permission, decided by an approver of the owning department, to read a few rows of a table’s locked columns for a few days, for a stated purpose. Holding a role is never enough on its own, apart from being an approver of the department that owns the data.

6
Devi
Devi tries to read the locked rows and is refused
Munitas console · Locked columns, opened · /versions/<id>/locked-rows

Devi brought the table in, but is not an approver of the Cardiology department, so the platform refuses and says why in its own words.

A red box reads “Could not read these rows.” and gives one reason: this person is not an approver of the department that owns this data and holds no current lease for its locked columns.
7
Devi
Devi writes why, and asks for five rows for three days
Munitas console · Version detail · Your access

The form asks for a purpose, a number of days and a number of rows. The platform states the limits itself, at most 7 days and at most 20 rows, and the purpose is recorded with the request. The rows are chosen by the platform, not by the person asking, and they are the same every time, so asking repeatedly cannot be used to read the whole table.

What you need them for holds Devi’s reason. For how many days (up to 7) reads 3, and How many rows (up to 20) reads 5. The small print reads The rows you can read are chosen for you and are the same every time you look, and Ask for access is ready.
8
Devi
The request waits for an approver
Munitas console · Version detail · Your access

Asking opens nothing. Devi still cannot read any locked value until an approver of the Cardiology department decides.

A yellow box reads “Your request is waiting for an approver.” and repeats the request: for 5 rows for 3 days, with Devi’s reason. A link reads See your requests.
9
Sam
Sam, a researcher, has no way to ask at all
Munitas console · Version detail · Your access

Sam holds the researcher role, which is for working with data that has already been de-identified, meaning the names, dates and other identifying detail have been taken out. Sam opens the same table and sees how it is built, but no value, and is not offered a form, because the locked values are not needed to work with the readable columns.

The box under Your access reads Your role cannot read the locked values and cannot ask for them. The table above it lists the same columns Devi saw, and there is no form.
PART THREE

Hartley, who answers for Cardiology, decides

The person who asks never decides. Only an approver of the department that owns the data can, and an approver of another department cannot.

10
Hartley
Hartley sees the request waiting
Munitas console · Locked-column access · /locked-column-access

Hartley is a data custodian and an approver of the Cardiology department, so the request about Cardiology data appears on this page. It shows who asked, why, how many rows and days, and offers Approve and Decline. A custodian of another department would see nothing here.

Under Waiting for you to decide there is one row: Devi, the reason, 5 rows, 3 days and the state Waiting for an approver, with a box reading A note, recorded with your decision. In force in your departments reads No leases in force.
11
Hartley
Hartley writes a note, and both buttons are ready
Munitas console · Locked-column access · Waiting for you to decide

The note is stored with the decision. A refusal needs a note, so that the person who asked is told why. Approving needs none, but a note makes the record easier to read later.

The note box holds “Five rows is enough for that.” and both Approve and Decline are ready to press.
12
Hartley
Hartley approves, and the lease is in force
Munitas console · Locked-column access · In force in your departments

The lease now lasts three days from the approval and opens five rows. Hartley can end it early at any time, and so can Devi.

Waiting for you to decide now reads No requests waiting for you. In force in your departments lists Devi, 5 rows, 3 days, the label In force, an end date three days after the approval, and Approved by Hartley with the note Five rows is enough for that. A button reads End now.
13
Hartley
Hartley reads the report on small groups
Munitas console · Version detail · Small groups

A small group is a combination of readable columns, such as postcode and age band, shared by only a few people, so that one of them could be singled out even though no column names anybody. The platform counts different people, not rows, because a person with several visits is still one person to find. The report is advice. It never stopped the table being sealed and shows no values. The approvers, the de-identification reviewer, the privacy auditor and the data protection officer, who watches how an organisation handles personal data, can read it, and only an approver can decide what to do about it.

A yellow box reads 12 of 20 people sit in a group smaller than 5. The smallest group holds 1 person. Two lines say what locking each column would leave: Locking postcode would leave 4 people in a small group and Locking age_band would leave 6 people in a small group. Below, “What will you do about it?” offers two choices, and Record this decision is greyed out until a reason is written.
14
Hartley
Hartley records what will be done, and why
Munitas console · Version detail · Small groups

Hartley chooses to change the contract before the next table is sealed, and writes why. The decision is made once, and the platform refuses to change it afterwards, even to somebody who writes to the database directly.

A line reads Decided by Hartley, then the date, the contract will change before the next table, and Hartley’s reason, The next contract version will lock the postcode. The decision form has gone.
PART FOUR

Devi reads the five rows the lease opens

A lease opens a fixed few rows for a short time. It does not open the table.

15
Devi
Devi now holds a lease
Munitas console · Version detail · Your access

The same section that showed a form now says what Devi holds: five of the 23 rows, until the lease ends, approved by Hartley for the stated reason. Devi can read the rows or end the lease personally.

A green box reads You hold a lease: 5 rows of 23, with the end date, and Approved by Hartley and the date, then for: followed by Devi’s reason. Two actions are offered: Read your 5 rows and End this lease now.
16
Devi
Devi reads five rows, with the locked values opened
Munitas console · Locked columns, opened · /versions/<id>/locked-rows

These are the only five rows Devi can read, and they are the same five every time. The locked values are opened for them: real names and reasons for visits. Every key that is opened for this is recorded, naming the person it belongs to by their person code. The other 18 rows stay locked.

A yellow banner reads Your lease opens 5 of 23 rows. They are the same rows every time, and a later lease opens the same ones. The table shows five rows with names under patient_name and reasons under reason_for_visit. The column patient_number (now a person code) holds labels that begin with T-.
PART FIVE

Marlow checks how locking was used, and sees no name

A privacy auditor is a person who checks how locked data was used. The role reads records of use and no personal data, and can ask for a lease like anybody else if it ever needs a real value.

17
Marlow
Marlow reads who read, who was refused, and under which lease
Munitas console · Locked data audit · /locking-audit

Marlow holds the privacy auditor role. The page lists every read of locked columns and every refusal, every lease with who asked and who decided, and the treatment of every column. People appear by name, and no value from any table appears at all. Reading this page is recorded too. Each time the capture for this page ran, Devi asked and read again, so the same story appears once for each run.

Who read locked columns, and who was refused lists Devi with Refused, the reason and asked without a lease, and with Read beside Devi’s purpose. Under Leases, Devi’s lease reads 5 rows for 3 days, with Approved by Hartley and the date under it. No patient name appears.
18
Marlow
Marlow sees how each table’s columns were treated, and the small groups
Munitas console · Locked data audit · How each table’s columns were treated, Small groups

For each table sealed under a privacy contract, the page lists its columns, how identifying each is and what was done to it, so an auditor can check that what the contract promised is what happened. The small groups table shows each finding and whether the owner decided anything about it.

Clinic appointments, version 1.0.0 lists patient_name and reason_for_visit as Locked under the person’s key. Under Small groups, each row reads postcode, age_band, 20 people and 12 (smaller than 5), and the last column reads Contract will change by Hartley or Not decided.
19
Marlow
Marlow sees every key that was opened, and by whom
Munitas console · Locked data audit · Keys

Each person has a key of their own. It is made when the person first appears in a table, opened when their locked values are read, and destroyed if they are ever erased. The list shows each opening with the time, who did it, and the person code, which means nothing on its own. The page shows the newest 25 lines first and turns the rest into pages.

Each line reads A key was opened, why (To read locked rows, under a lease), the table, the time, Devi and a person code beginning with T-. At the foot of the list Previous and Next turn the pages, and Lines per page sets how many lines a page holds.

Captured live against the health organisation by web/walkthroughs/locked-columns.spec.ts and built by docs/tools/build_locked_columns_walkthrough.py. Every person and number in the two files is invented, and the files themselves are in web/walkthroughs/fixtures/locked-appointments/. What the platform refuses here is proved separately by verify/v129_locked_column_leases.py, verify/v130_group_size_reports.py and verify/v133_seal_table_from_files.py. Every person, patient and card holder in the example data is invented.
